owner.occupation: Buyer for a group of London museum shops

world.bio: I buy for the shops of four London museums, which means I spend my days in showrooms, studios and trade fairs deciding what a visitor will want to take home at the end of a gallery visit. I trained in textile conservation, left the bench because I was bad at being quiet, and have a lasting dislike of mass-made 'heritage'. I'd rather sell one honest object than ten things with a crest on them.
skills_assets: Buying budget and shelf space across four museum shops, with two seasonal ranges a year
A little black notebook of about two hundred makers worldwide, many reached through personal introductions
Training in textile conservation, so she can tell hand embroidery from machine at arm's length
Knows the retail compliance side: plastic-free packaging rules, labelling, safety paperwork
Relationships with three small London printers who do maker-story cards

projects.name: Spring/Summer buying round
projects.text: Closing the gift-shop orders for spring. Trying to cut the proportion of generic 'heritage' stock from around forty percent to under twenty. Meetings with eleven suppliers between now and mid-November.

projects.name: 'Hands of Asia' range for next year
projects.text: A themed range tied to a spring exhibition. I want objects that carry a named maker. The brief is thin on volume but strict on provenance, and merchandising is already asking for numbers I can't give them yet.

projects.name: Narrowboat restoration
projects.text: Weekends on a 1962 narrowboat in a Hertfordshire marina. Currently stripping the cabin sides. I've learned that paint remover gets everywhere.

notes.text: Trade fair at the NEC, day two. Walked past a hundred stands of 'artisan' goods all made in the same factory. One stall sold a hand-printed scarf that I could tell was digital at ten feet. The owner told me proudly it was 'heritage-style'. I smiled and said no thank you. I wrote in my book: museum shops want objects with a named maker, not 'heritage-style' stock. Putting that on a slide for the next buying meeting.
Daughter Maya's GCSE mock results came back. Maths is shaky. She says she can't stand being told it will be fine. I said all right, I won't say it, but I'll make dinner. She smiled, a bit.

Narrowboat. Spent four hours on the left side of the cabin. The old green paint has a layer of something yellow under it and I can't tell if it's lead. Will get a test kit. Marina neighbour Colin handed me a flask of tea without being asked and I've decided he's the best man in Hertfordshire.

Meeting with merchandising. They want volumes and price points for 'Hands of Asia' by 15 October. I said the range needs maker-signed embroidery, at least three hundred units a batch, English maker-story cards, and packaging that passes our plastic-free rules. They asked who can do all of that. I said nobody I have yet. Single makers can't reach three hundred; the agencies who can reach it can't show me the person who made the thing.
Japanese lesson on the Tube. Learned 'tegami' means letter and 'te' means hand, which is the right word to have on a day like today. My accent is a disaster; a man across from me raised an eyebrow.
The narrowboat engine started. Only briefly, then died. Colin said that's progress. I danced on the deck. Someone from the next boat clapped.
Reading about Karen weaving and Hmong stitch work. Not for work yet. It is possible I'm only reading because I like the pictures.
Interview with a ceramics studio in Stoke. Lovely people, lovely pots, very slow response to email. Might not be right for a retail cycle but I'll keep the number.

messages.text:
Maya: Mum, can you not mention my mock results at dinner with Gran.
Me: I won't.
Maya: Promise.
Me: Promise. I'll talk about the boat instead.

Tom: Eleanor, any update on Hands of Asia volumes?
Me: Not yet. I need makers, not a catalogue.
Tom: We can't fill a shelf with one-offs.
Me: I know. That's the problem.

Rachel: Mum's asking whether you're coming to Sunday lunch.
Me: Yes, I'll bring the apple tart.
Rachel: Are you bringing Maya?
Me: She says yes if there's no maths talk.

Colin: Engine's alright, but the bilge pump's on its way out.
Me: How long?
Colin: A month, maybe two.
Me: I'll order one.

calendar.event: Merchandising deadline: Hands of Asia volumes and price points
Supplier meeting, textile studio in Spitalfields
Last buying meeting of the autumn round

relations.about: Marina neighbour on the next narrowboat, retired boat-builder, brings tea
Daughter, fifteen, doing GCSEs, hates being told it will be fine
Head of merchandising, practical, always asks for volumes

constraints: Won't buy goods whose maker can't be named
Packaging must meet the shop group's plastic-free rules
Merchandising needs batch sizes and lead times before it will commit to a range
sensitive: Is quietly worried the 'Hands of Asia' range will be filled with the very generic stock she hates because she cannot find volume
Does not feel good at parenting a teenager
